On the Tuesday of Passion Week, sitting on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Jesus told four of his disciples that the building they admired would be torn down stone by stone, and then answered their questions about when and how. The Olivet Discourse (Matthew 24–25; Mark 13; Luke 21:5–36) is the longest prophecy Jesus gave, and almost every view of the end times is shaped by how it is read. This study sets the discourse in its first-century world: Herod's temple, Roman rule, Zealot unrest, the early church's mission, and the Jewish War of AD 66–73 as Josephus, Tacitus and others recorded it. It walks through Matthew 24 unit by unit, showing how partial preterists, full preterists, dispensationalists, historic premillennialists, amillennialists, historicists, idealists and spiritual readers each understand the verses, at their strongest. Alongside each unit it sets out the historical evidence offered for an AD 70 fulfilment and the textual evidence offered for a still-future one, and it flags where scholars dispute the matches. The aim is not to decide the question for you but to let you weigh the strongest case each side can make.
Herod's temple and its stones

The temple the disciples pointed to was the Second Temple as rebuilt and vastly enlarged by Herod the Great, a project begun around 20/19 BC and still under way in Jesus' day (John 2:20 speaks of forty-six years of building). Josephus describes white stones of enormous size, some about 25 cubits long, 8 high and 12 wide in one account, and 45 cubits long in another, along with gold-plated facades that dazzled anyone approaching the city. The platform was doubled in size by massive retaining walls, parts of which, including the Western Wall, still stand. The work on the wider complex was only finished under the procurator Albinus around AD 63–64, when Josephus says some eighteen thousand workmen were laid off, just six years before the whole was destroyed. For a first-century Jew the temple was the dwelling of God's name, the centre of sacrifice and pilgrimage, and the symbol of Israel's identity, so a prediction of its total ruin was shocking. Earlier prophets had warned of the first temple's destruction (Jeremiah 7:12–14; 26:18; Micah 3:12), and Jesus' words echo that prophetic pattern of judgment on a faithless house. Because the temple platform's lower courses survived, readers debate whether “not one stone upon another” refers to the sanctuary buildings themselves, which were completely dismantled, or is proverbial language for total ruin.
Judea under Rome and the procurators

Judea came under direct Roman rule in AD 6, when Archelaus was deposed and a census under Quirinius provoked the revolt of Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:37). From then on, apart from the brief reign of Agrippa I (AD 41–44), the region was governed by equestrian prefects and procurators such as Pontius Pilate (26–36), Felix (c. 52–60), Festus (c. 60–62), Albinus (62–64) and Gessius Florus (64–66). Josephus portrays most of them as corrupt or provocative: Pilate brought standards bearing the emperor's image into Jerusalem, Cumanus' soldier exposed himself in the temple court at Passover, and Florus seized seventeen talents from the temple treasury and let troops loose on the city. In AD 40 the emperor Gaius (Caligula) ordered his statue set up in the temple, a crisis averted only by delay and his assassination, which many think kept the fear of a new “abomination” alive in Jewish and Christian minds. Taxation, land pressure, banditry and conflicts between Jews and Gentiles in mixed cities such as Caesarea all raised tension through the 50s and 60s. Tacitus, a Roman with no sympathy for the Jews, still admits that their patience lasted until Florus. This is the world in which Jesus' warnings about wars, rumours of wars, betrayal and flight would first have been heard and remembered.
Zealots, sicarii and messianic pretenders

Josephus describes a “fourth philosophy” founded by Judas the Galilean that refused to acknowledge any master but God, and from the 50s onward the sicarii, “dagger-men”, assassinated opponents in festival crowds, beginning with the high priest Jonathan. He also records a string of figures who promised signs of deliverance: Theudas, who under the procurator Fadus (c. AD 44–46) led a crowd to the Jordan promising to part it; impostors who led people into the wilderness under Felix; and “the Egyptian”, who gathered followers on the Mount of Olives to watch Jerusalem's walls fall. Acts mentions both Theudas (5:36) and the Egyptian with his four thousand men of the sicarii (21:38); Josephus gives a larger figure of thirty thousand, and Acts places its Theudas before Judas the Galilean, a chronological puzzle scholars resolve in different ways. During the war itself, leaders such as Menahem, John of Gischala and Simon bar Giora acted as rival kings or deliverers, and Josephus says a false prophet promised “signs of deliverance” in the temple on the day it burned. Preterists argue that this cluster of deceivers fits Jesus' warnings about false christs and false prophets with signs and wonders (Matthew 24:5, 11, 23–26) remarkably well. Futurists reply that false messiahs have appeared in every age and that the discourse points to a climactic deceiver still to come. Either way, the term “Zealot” as a defined party is best attested for the war years (from about AD 66–68), so care is needed not to read it back into Jesus' own day.
The early church's mission and persecution before AD 70

Between Pentecost and the war, the church spread from Jerusalem through Judea, Samaria, Syria, Asia Minor, Greece and Rome, exactly the arc that Acts traces and that Paul's letters assume. Paul could write in the late 50s and early 60s that the Romans' faith was proclaimed “in all the world” (Romans 1:8), that the message had gone out to the ends of the oikoumenē (Romans 10:18, quoting Psalm 19:4), and that the gospel had been proclaimed “in all creation under heaven” (Colossians 1:23). Persecution came in waves: the arrest of the apostles (Acts 4–5), Stephen's death and the scattering (Acts 7–8), the execution of James son of Zebedee by Agrippa I around AD 44 (Acts 12:2), the stoning of James the Lord's brother in AD 62 (Antiquities 20.9.1), and Nero's savage punishment of Christians after the fire of Rome in AD 64 (Tacitus, Annals 15.44). Believers were handed over to councils, beaten in synagogues and brought before governors and kings (Acts 22–26), as Jesus had said in Mark 13:9 and Matthew 10:17–18. Internal troubles also surface: apostasy, false teachers and love growing cold are recurring themes in the letters (2 Timothy 4:10; 2 Peter 2:1; Revelation 2:4). Preterists see in this a point-by-point fulfilment of Matthew 24:9–14 within a generation. Futurists and amillennialists agree these things happened but hold that they began a pattern which continues and climaxes before Christ's return.
Josephus as witness, and his biases

Flavius Josephus, a priest and aristocrat, commanded Jewish forces in Galilee in 67, surrendered at Jotapata, predicted that Vespasian would become emperor, and spent the rest of the war in the Roman camp, watching the siege of Jerusalem from outside its walls. He wrote the Jewish War in the 70s under Flavian patronage, and the Antiquities around AD 93–94, so he is an eyewitness of much of what he describes, which is why every reading of the Olivet Discourse quotes him. He also had clear agendas: he blames the disaster on a small band of “tyrants” and brigands rather than the nation, presents Titus as merciful and eager to save the temple, and portrays the Romans as instruments of God's judgment. Later Christian writer Sulpicius Severus, probably drawing on a lost part of Tacitus, says Titus actually wanted the temple destroyed, which suggests Josephus softened his patron's role. His numbers, such as 1,100,000 dead in the siege, are widely judged to be inflated, though the scale of the catastrophe is not in doubt. Josephus was not a Christian and had no motive to make events match Jesus' words, which preterists see as making the correspondences more striking; critics note that some parallels depend on selecting and arranging his material. Readers should therefore use him as an invaluable but partisan source, checking him against Tacitus, Suetonius, Dio Cassius, archaeology and coins where possible.
The Jewish War of AD 66–73 and the fall of Jerusalem

The war broke out in AD 66 after Florus' plunder of the temple treasury and the massacre that followed; the captain of the temple, Eleazar son of Ananias, stopped the daily sacrifices offered for the emperor, which Josephus calls the true start of the war. Cestius Gallus, governor of Syria, marched on Jerusalem in the autumn of 66, broke into the suburbs, then withdrew unexpectedly and was routed at Beth-horon; Josephus says many leading citizens left the city at that point. Vespasian subdued Galilee in 67 and much of Judea in 68, but Nero's suicide in June 68 and the civil wars of 69 (the “year of the four emperors”) paused operations while factions inside Jerusalem fought each other and burned the grain stores. Titus began the siege at Passover in AD 70, surrounded the city with a wall of circumvallation, and starved it into weakness; the temple was burned in the month Ab (late August), the upper city fell in September, and the walls and buildings were then razed. Tacitus says six hundred thousand were besieged; Josephus' totals are higher and disputed, but tens of thousands certainly died and many were enslaved. Titus' triumph in Rome in 71 displayed the temple's menorah and table, still visible on the Arch of Titus, and the last stronghold, Masada, fell in 73 or 74. For Jews it meant the end of sacrifice and priesthood; for Christians it became, for many, the clearest vindication of Jesus' words about the temple.
Apocalyptic “cosmic” language in the prophets

Matthew 24:29 draws its words about the sun darkened, the moon not giving its light and the stars falling almost directly from Isaiah 13:10 and 34:4. In their original settings those oracles announce the fall of Babylon (Isaiah 13) and of Edom and the nations (Isaiah 34); similar language is used for Egypt (Ezekiel 32:7–8), for a locust invasion and the day of the Lord on Judah (Joel 2:10, 31), and for Israel's own judgment (Amos 8:9; Jeremiah 4:23–28). Many interpreters, from Calvin and Thomas Newton to R. T. France and N. T. Wright, conclude that ancient readers heard such words as the poetry of political and covenantal upheaval, the “heavens” of a nation's rulers being shaken, rather than as astronomical forecasts. Peter's use of Joel 2 at Pentecost, applying sun-and-moon signs to events then taking place (Acts 2:16–21), is cited as a New Testament example. Futurists answer that the prophets' day-of-the-Lord oracles also look past local judgments to a final, universal one (Isaiah 13:9–11 speaks of punishing “the world”), that Jesus places these signs “in the heavens” and links them to a visible coming, and that Revelation 6:12–14 and 2 Peter 3:10–12 continue the same imagery for the end. Many moderate readers hold that the language can be both symbolic of historical judgment and a pointer to the final cosmic renewal. How one hears this language is probably the single biggest factor in how one reads 24:29–31.
The audience: “you” and the date of Matthew

Jesus speaks privately to Peter, James, John and Andrew (Mark 13:3) and repeatedly uses the second person: “see that no one leads you astray”, “they will deliver you up”, “when you see”, “pray that your flight may not be in winter”. Preterists argue that a natural reading of these pronouns makes the disciples themselves the people who would see the signs, and that the local details (Judea, housetops, the Sabbath, fleeing to the mountains) suit first-century Palestine. Futurists reply that Jesus often addresses the disciples as representatives of later believers (Matthew 28:20, “to the end of the age”), so the second person need not limit the horizon to their lifetime. Matthew's Gospel was written for largely Jewish-Christian readers concerned with the Law, the temple and the relationship of the church to Israel, but its date is disputed. Early tradition (Papias in Eusebius, Church History 3.39.16; Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.1.1) puts Matthew first and early, and scholars such as J. A. T. Robinson, R. H. Gundry and D. A. Carson argue for a date before AD 70; the majority of critical scholars prefer AD 80–90, partly because they read the discourse and the wedding-feast parable (22:7, “burned their city”) as written after the event. If Matthew wrote before 70, the discourse was a warning his readers still had to heed; if after, he wrote to show that Jesus' prediction had come true, and that Jesus' final coming was still to be awaited. Either way, the parenthesis “let the reader understand” (24:15) shows the evangelist pressing the warning on his own readers.

Jesus' prediction that not one stone would be left on another prompted the disciples' question, and how one reads their question governs how one reads the answer. In Matthew it has two or three parts: when will “these things” be, and what will be the sign of “your coming” (parousia) and “the end of the age” (synteleia tou aiōnos)? Mark and Luke record only the question about the temple and its sign. Some argue the disciples assumed the temple's fall, Christ's coming and the end of the age were one event, and that Jesus' answer either confirms that (full preterism), separates them (futurism, dispensationalism, many partial preterists after 24:36), or merges near and far (amillennial and historic premillennial double reference). Others note that in Jewish usage “the age” could mean the present era of history before the age to come, or, as preterists propose, the old covenant age that ended with the temple.
Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the end of the age?
Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?
Teacher, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when these things are about to take place?

The question arises from the temple prophecy, so “these things” and the sign point first to AD 70. Matthew 24:4–34 answers it: every sign, the abomination, the tribulation and even the Son of Man's coming on the clouds (Daniel 7:13 language for vindication and judgment) fall within “this generation”. Most partial preterists (France, Gentry, Sproul, DeMar) see a transition at 24:36, “But concerning that day and hour”, to the final bodily coming and judgment, which has no signs and no time limit; Kik placed it at 24:35/36, and a few put it at 25:31. The “end of the age” is then the close of the old covenant era marked by the temple's fall.

There is one question with linked parts and one answer. The coming, the end of the age and the temple's fall are the same event, and the whole discourse through 25:46 was fulfilled in AD 66–70, including the parousia, the resurrection-gathering and the judgment. Full preterists say any division at 24:36 is inconsistent, since the parousia appears on both sides (24:27, 37, 39). This view lies outside the historic creeds, which confess a future bodily return, a point its critics press.

The disciples asked about two different things, and Luke 21:12–24 answers the first (the AD 70 destruction), while Matthew 24:4–31 chiefly answers the second, describing the future seventieth week of Daniel 9:27. Verses 4–14 are the first half of the tribulation (or general signs), 24:15 its midpoint when the Antichrist desecrates a rebuilt temple, 24:21–28 the great tribulation, and 24:29–31 the visible Second Coming to rescue believing Israel and set up the kingdom. The church, raptured beforehand, is not directly addressed; the disciples stand for the Jewish remnant of that future time.

Broadly futurist readers, not all dispensational, hold that whatever partial fulfilment AD 70 provides, the signs, the great tribulation, the cosmic signs and the coming in 24:4–31 culminate in a future crisis just before Christ's return. They stress that the parousia elsewhere in the New Testament is the bodily, visible return (1 Thessalonians 4:15; 2 Thessalonians 2:1–8) and that the disciples' question about the “end of the age” is answered with “the end” (24:6, 14), which Jesus distinguishes from the temple's fall.

Jesus answers both questions with one prophetic perspective in which the near judgment on Jerusalem and the final crisis are seen together, like mountain peaks seen from a distance. Luke 21 especially shows the fall of Jerusalem followed by the “times of the Gentiles” and then the coming. Historic premillennialists such as Ladd and Blomberg take 24:29–31 as the single posttribulational return, at which the church is gathered, so the discourse is addressed to the church as well as to Israel.

The discourse deliberately interweaves the two horizons, AD 70 and the end, because the first is a type and foretaste of the second. Many signs (deception, wars, persecution, gospel preaching) characterise the whole age between the comings, intensifying before the end; the abomination and flight fit AD 70; the coming of 24:30–31 and all of 24:36–25:46 refer to the final return. Some amillennialists (Riddlebarger) accept a preterist reading of more of 24:4–34, while others (Hoekema) emphasise the double reference.

Classical historicists such as Thomas Newton and Albert Barnes read 24:4–28 largely as AD 70, often with detailed appeals to Josephus, and then saw the long era after it as a continuous history running to the end. Luke's “times of the Gentiles” is that long era, and Adventist historicists place the great tribulation in the papal persecutions (1260 years, usually 538–1798) and the signs of 24:29 in events such as the Lisbon earthquake (1755), the Dark Day (1780) and the meteor shower of 1833, before a future visible advent.
